hello.title: Hello, Scheme!
hello.summary: Write your first Scheme program, print with display and newline, and calculate in prefix notation.
hello.lesson.0: A Scheme program is a list of expressions. An expression in parentheses is a **procedure call**: the first item is the procedure, the other items are its arguments. The procedure `display` shows a value, and `newline` ends the line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Scheme!"`, is a **string**.
hello.lesson.2: `display` takes one value and does not start a new line. Several calls of `display` print on the same line. `(newline)` is a call without arguments, but it still needs its parentheses. Numbers are written without quotes.
hello.lesson.5: In mathematics you write `1 + 2`. In Scheme the operator comes first, like every other procedure: `(+ 1 2)`. This is called **prefix notation**. The procedures `+` (add), `-` (subtract) and `*` (multiply) accept several arguments: `(+ 1 2 3)` is `6`, and `(- 10 2 3)` is 10 − 2 − 3, so `5`.
hello.lesson.7: You can put expressions inside other expressions. Scheme first calculates the inner ones. There are no precedence rules to remember: the parentheses show the order.
hello.lesson.9: Every opening parenthesis `(` needs a closing one `)`. Do not add extra parentheses either: `((+ 1 2))` is an error, because Scheme tries to call the result `3` as a procedure.
hello.lesson.10: In a strict R7RS program, the first line imports the standard libraries, for example `(import (scheme base) (scheme write))`. Many Scheme systems load them for you, so the examples in this course leave this line out. If your Scheme says that `display` is unknown, add the line at the top.
hello-2.explain: The inner expression comes first: `(- 7 2)` is 5. Then `(* 3 5)` is 15.
hello-3.prompt: How do you write 5 + 3 in Scheme?
hello-3.explain: The procedure always comes first inside the parentheses, and `+` is a procedure.
hello-4.explain: `display` adds no space and no line break. Only `(newline)` ends a line.
hello-5.explain: `-` subtracts every later argument from the first one: 10 − 2 − 3 is 5.
hello-6.statement: `(display "Hi")` starts a new line after the text.
hello-6.explain: `display` never ends the line. You need `(newline)` for that.
hello-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 10.
hello-7.explain: `(* 2 5)` multiplies and gives 10. `+` would give 7 and `-` would give -3.
hello-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Hi` and `Bo` on two lines.
hello-8.explain: `(newline)` ends the first line. `display` needs a value, and `line` does not exist.
hello-9.prompt: Build a line that prints the result of 4 times 5.
hello-9.explain: `(* 4 5)` multiplies, and `display` prints the result. The procedure always comes first.
hello-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Sum: 6`.
hello-10.explain: First the text, then the result of `(+ 1 2 3)`, then the end of the line. The calculation is the argument of the second `display`.
hello-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-12.explain: A closing parenthesis is missing. The line must be `(display (+ 2 3))`.
values.title: Values
values.summary: Work with exact and inexact numbers, strings, symbols and booleans, and give values a name with define.
values.lesson.0: Scheme keeps numbers **exact** when it can. Whole numbers and fractions are exact: `(/ 6 4)` gives the fraction `3/2`, not `1.5`. You can also write a fraction like `3/4` directly. A number with a decimal point, like `2.5`, is **inexact**, and a calculation with an inexact number gives an inexact result.
values.lesson.2: `inexact` turns an exact number into a decimal number, and `exact` turns it back. For whole-number division, `quotient` gives the whole part and `remainder` gives what is left over.
values.lesson.5: `display` shows a string without its quotes. `write` shows a value the way you write it in code, so a string keeps its quotes. A **symbol** is a name used as a value. You write it with a quote mark in front: `'apple`. The quote tells Scheme to use the name itself instead of looking up its value.
values.lesson.6: The two **booleans** are `#t` (true) and `#f` (false). Comparisons give a boolean: `(< 2 3)` asks whether 2 is less than 3.
values.lesson.9: `(define name value)` gives a value a name. After that, you use the name instead of the value. Names may contain letters, digits and signs like `-` and `?`, for example `item-price`.
values.lesson.11: `string-append` joins several strings into one. It only accepts strings, so `number->string` first turns a number into a string. The arrow `->` in the name means "to".
values.lesson.13: Strings and numbers do not mix: `(+ "1" 2)` and `(string-append "Age: " 36)` are errors. Convert the number first with `number->string`.
values.card.3: `(define price 4)` gives the value `4` the name `price`
values-1.explain: Dividing two exact numbers gives an exact fraction: 10/4 is reduced to `5/2`.
values-2.explain: 23 is 5 times 4 plus 3, so the remainder is 3.
values-3.explain: The names stand for their values: 5 + 7 + 5 is 17.
values-4.explain: `write` shows a string the way you write it in code, with its double quotes.
values-5.explain: A quote mark in front of a name makes a symbol. `"apple"` is a string, `#t` a boolean and `3/4` a number.
values-6.explain: Both numbers are exact, so the result is the exact fraction `1/2`.
values-7.explain: `inexact` turns the exact fraction `1/4` into the decimal number `0.25`.
values-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Total: 12`.
values-8.explain: `string-append` needs strings, and `number->string` turns the number 12 into the string `"12"`.
values-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3.
values-9.explain: `quotient` gives the whole part of 17 divided by 5, which is 3. `remainder` would give 2 and `/` the fraction `17/5`.
values-10.prompt: Build a line that gives the value 8 the name `width`.
values-10.explain: `(define width 8)`: first `define`, then the name, then the value.
values-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 12.
values-11.explain: A name must be defined before it is used: `height` needs `width`, and `area` needs both.
values-12.explain: `string-append` only accepts strings. Use `(number->string age)` instead of `age`.
functions.title: Procedures
functions.summary: Write your own procedures with define and lambda, and create local names with let and let*.
functions.lesson.0: A **procedure** is a piece of code with a name that you can call again and again. `(define (double x) (* 2 x))` defines the procedure `double` with one **parameter** `x`. The value of the last expression in the body is the result. Scheme has no `return` keyword.
functions.lesson.2: A procedure can have several parameters. Its body can also contain several expressions, for example `display` and `newline`. They run one after the other.
functions.lesson.5: `lambda` creates a procedure without a name: `(lambda (x) (* 3 x))` takes `x` and gives three times `x`. In fact, `(define (triple x) ...)` is a short way to write `(define triple (lambda (x) ...))`. You can also call a `lambda` directly.
functions.lesson.8: `let` creates names that exist only inside its body: `(let ((name value) ...) body)`. Each `(name value)` pair is called a **binding**. Note the double parentheses around the list of bindings.
functions.lesson.10: In a `let`, the bindings cannot see each other. `let*` creates them one after the other, so a later binding can use an earlier one.
functions.lesson.12: Parentheses around a name always mean a call. `double` is the procedure itself, `(double 4)` calls it. `(double)` is an error, because `double` needs one argument.
functions.card.1: The value of the last expression in the body is the result
functions.card.2: `(lambda (x) (* 3 x))` is a procedure without a name
functions.card.4: `let*` lets later bindings use earlier ones
functions-1.explain: `x` is 5 in this call, so the body gives 5 + 10.
functions-2.explain: The arguments go to the parameters in order: `a` is 3 and `b` is 10, so 3 − 10 is -7.
functions-3.explain: The `lambda` is called directly with 3: 3 × 3 × 3 is 27.
functions-4.prompt: Which line defines a procedure `inc` that adds 1 to its argument?
functions-4.explain: The name and the parameters go together in parentheses after `define`, then comes the body.
functions-5.explain: Inside `show`, `(display x)` prints 4. The result of `show` is 8, which the outer `display` prints right after it.
functions-6.explain: `let*` creates `a` first, so `b` can use it: 2 × 3 is 6.
functions-7.explain: In a `let`, the binding of `b` cannot see `a`, so this is an error. Use `let*` instead.
functions-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 5.
functions-8.explain: Half of a number is the number divided by 2: `(/ 10 2)` is 5.
functions-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 8.
functions-9.explain: `lambda` creates the procedure, and `define` gives it the name `cube`.
functions-10.prompt: Build the first line of a procedure `area` with the parameters `w` and `h`.
functions-10.explain: The name and the parameters go together in parentheses: `(define (area w h)`.
functions-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 77.
functions-11.explain: The `let` creates `tax` before its body `(+ price tax)` uses it, and the procedure must be defined before it is called.
functions-12.explain: `greet` has one parameter, so the call needs one argument, for example `(greet "Ana")`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Compare values, use predicates like zero?, and choose with if, cond and case, and, or and not.
conditions.lesson.0: Comparisons give a boolean: `=` (equal numbers), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. A **predicate** is a procedure that answers a yes-or-no question. Its name usually ends with `?`, for example `zero?`, `even?`, `odd?`, `positive?` and `negative?`.
conditions.lesson.3: `(if test then else)` checks the test. If it is true, the result is the `then` part, otherwise the `else` part. In Scheme only `#f` is false. Every other value counts as true, even `0` and the empty string `""`.
conditions.lesson.6: `cond` handles several cases. Each clause is `(test result)`. Scheme checks the tests from top to bottom, and the first true test wins. The last clause can start with `else`: it catches everything else.
conditions.lesson.8: `case` compares one value with lists of constants, such as numbers or symbols. The first list that contains the value wins.
conditions.lesson.11: `(and a b)` is true when all its arguments are true. `(or a b)` is true when at least one is true. `(not a)` turns `#t` into `#f` and the other way round. `and` and `or` stop as soon as the answer is known.
conditions.lesson.13: `=` only compares numbers. To compare strings or other values, use `equal?`: `(equal? "cat" "cat")` is `#t`.
conditions.card.0: `(if test then else)`; only `#f` counts as false
conditions.card.1: `(cond (test1 r1) (test2 r2) (else r3))`: the first true test wins
conditions-1.explain: 3 is not greater than 5, so the test is `#f` and `if` gives the `else` part.
conditions-2.explain: Both tests are false for 0, so the `else` clause gives `"zero"`.
conditions-3.explain: `(odd? 3)` is true, but `(> 3 5)` is false. `and` needs all arguments to be true.
conditions-4.explain: Only `#f` is false in Scheme. The empty string counts as true, so `if` gives `'a`.
conditions-5.explain: 5 is in the list `(4 5 6)`, so `case` gives the symbol `medium`.
conditions-6.explain: The first true test wins. `(>= p 50)` is already true, so the code prints `C`. Put the largest limit first.
conditions-7.statement: In Scheme, `0` counts as false in an `if`.
conditions-7.explain: Only `#f` is false. `0` is a normal value and counts as true.
conditions-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `#t`.
conditions-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `other`.
conditions-9.explain: A clause that starts with `else` catches every case that no earlier test matched.
conditions-10.prompt: Build a line that prints `yes` when `n` is greater than 10 and `no` otherwise.
conditions-10.explain: `if` takes the test first, then the result for true, then the result for false.
conditions-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `fizzbuzz`.
conditions-11.explain: 30 can be divided by 15 and by 3. The test for 15 must come first, because the first true test wins, and `else` is always last.
conditions-12.explain: Scheme has no `=<` procedure. "Less than or equal" is written `<=`: `(if (<= age 17)`.
lists.title: Lists
lists.summary: Build lists with list, cons and quote, take them apart with car and cdr, and use null?, length and append.
lists.lesson.0: A **list** holds values in order. `(list 1 2 3)` creates a list, and `display` shows it as `(1 2 3)`. You can also write a list with a quote mark: `'(1 2 3)`. Like with symbols, the quote tells Scheme to take the list as data instead of calling it. `length` counts the elements.
lists.lesson.3: `car` gives the first element of a list. `cdr` gives the rest: the list without its first element. The names are historical. `cadr` is short for the `car` of the `cdr`, so it gives the second element.
lists.lesson.5: `cons` puts a new element in front of a list: `(cons 0 '(1 2))` is `(0 1 2)`. Every list ends with the **empty list** `'()`. The predicate `null?` checks whether a list is empty.
lists.lesson.8: `append` joins lists into one list. `reverse` gives the elements in the opposite order. `list-ref` gets the element at a position. Positions start at 0.
lists.lesson.10: `car` and `cdr` of the empty list are errors. Check with `null?` first when a list can be empty.
lists.lesson.11: When the second argument of `cons` is not a list, the result is a **pair**, not a list. Scheme shows a pair with a dot between its two parts. A list is a chain of pairs that ends with `'()`.
lists.card.1: `(car l)` first element, `(cdr l)` the rest, `(cadr l)` the second
lists-2.explain: `append` joins the lists into `(1 2 3 4 5 6)`, which has 6 elements.
lists-3.explain: The list has only one element. Without it, the empty list `()` is left.
lists-4.explain: Positions start at 0: `a` is 0, `b` is 1 and `c` is 2.
lists-5.explain: `cons` puts 1 in front of `(2 3)`. The other expressions give `((1 2) . 3)`, `((1 2) 3)` and `(3 2 1)`.
lists-6.explain: `cdr` gives the rest of the list, which is the list `(2 3)`. The second element alone is `(cadr '(1 2 3))`.
lists-7.explain: `(cdr '(9))` is the empty list, so `null?` gives `#t`.
lists-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `(0 1 2)`.
lists-8.explain: `cons` puts 0 in front of the list. `list` would give `(0 (1 2))`.
lists-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `pear`.
lists-9.explain: `pear` is the second element, and `cadr` gives the second element.
lists-10.prompt: Build a line that prints the list `nums` in reverse order.
lists-10.explain: `(reverse nums)` gives the reversed list, and `display` prints it.
lists-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
lists-11.pairs.1: the list without its first element
lists-11.pairs.2: puts x in front of the list
lists-11.pairs.3: checks whether the list is empty
lists-12.prompt: The program should print `red` and `blue`. Which line has the bug?
lists-12.explain: Three `cdr` calls leave the empty list, and `car` of the empty list is an error. Two are enough: `(car (cdr (cdr colors)))`.
recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.summary: Repeat work with procedures that call themselves, walk through lists, and loop with tail calls and named let.
recursion.lesson.0: In Scheme you usually repeat work with **recursion**: a procedure calls itself. Every recursive procedure needs a **base case** that stops the recursion, and a step that brings the problem closer to the base case.
recursion.lesson.2: `(factorial 3)` is 3 × `(factorial 2)`, which is 3 × 2 × `(factorial 1)`, which is 3 × 2 × 1 × `(factorial 0)`. The base case `(factorial 0)` gives 1, so the result is 6.
recursion.lesson.4: Lists and recursion fit well together. The empty list is the base case. Otherwise you handle the `car` and let the recursion handle the `cdr`.
recursion.lesson.6: To build a new list, `cons` the result for the first element onto the result for the rest. The base case gives the empty list.
recursion.lesson.9: In `factorial`, a multiplication is still waiting after the recursive call, so Scheme must remember every step. When a call is the very last thing a procedure does, it is a **tail call**. Scheme guarantees that tail calls need no extra memory, so they work like a loop. An extra parameter, often called an **accumulator**, collects the result on the way.
recursion.lesson.11: A **named let** gives a loop a name: `(let loop ((i 1)) ...)` creates a local procedure `loop` with the parameter `i`, which starts at 1. Calling `(loop (+ i 1))` runs the next round. `when` runs its body only if the test is true. Unlike `if`, it has no `else` part and can contain several expressions.
recursion.lesson.13: Without a base case, or with a step that does not bring the problem closer to it, the recursion never stops.
recursion.card.0: A recursive procedure calls itself and needs a base case
recursion.card.2: A tail call is the last thing a procedure does and needs no extra memory
recursion.card.3: `(let loop ((i 0)) ... (loop (+ i 1)))` is a named let
recursion.card.4: `(when test expr ...)` runs the expressions only if the test is true
recursion-1.explain: The calls go 3, 2, 1, 0. At 0 the base case gives the symbol `go`.
recursion-3.explain: Every element adds 1, and the empty list gives 0: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 is 4.
recursion-4.explain: The loop adds `i` for 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, which gives 10. Then `i` is 5 and the total is printed.
recursion-5.prompt: What is missing in this procedure?
recursion-5.options.0: a base case for the empty list
recursion-5.explain: Without a base case, the recursion reaches the empty list and calls `car` on it, which is an error. Add `(if (null? l) 0 ...)`.
recursion-6.prompt: In which expression is the recursive call a tail call?
recursion-6.explain: In the other expressions, `*`, `+` or `cons` still has work to do after the recursive call returns.
recursion-7.explain: `f` counts down from 10 to 0, and the base case gives 0.
recursion-8.prompt: Complete the base case so the code prints 6.
recursion-8.explain: The sum of an empty list is 0. With 1 the result would be 7, and `'()` cannot be added to a number.
recursion-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `321`.
recursion-9.explain: The name after `let` is the name of the loop procedure. The body calls `(loop (- i 1))`, so the name must be `loop`.
recursion-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `(1 2)`.
recursion-10.explain: The base case gives the empty list. Otherwise the first element is put in front of the copy of the rest.
recursion-11.statement: The procedure `factorial` from the lesson uses a tail call.
recursion-11.explain: After `(factorial (- n 1))` returns, the result must still be multiplied by `n`, so the call is not the last thing that happens.
recursion-12.prompt: The program should print 24. Which line has the bug?
recursion-12.explain: The base case must give 1. With 0, every product becomes 0.
higher.title: Higher-order procedures
higher.summary: Pass procedures as values, use map, for-each and apply, and write your own filter procedure.
higher.lesson.0: Procedures are values, like numbers and strings. You can give them names, pass them as arguments and return them from other procedures. A procedure that takes or returns a procedure is called **higher-order**.
higher.lesson.3: `map` calls a procedure for every element of a list and gives a new list with the results. With two lists, `map` takes one element from each list for every call.
higher.lesson.5: `for-each` also calls a procedure for every element, but it gives no useful result. You use it for actions such as printing.
higher.lesson.7: `apply` calls a procedure with the elements of a list as its arguments: `(apply + '(1 2 3))` is the same as `(+ 1 2 3)`. `max` gives the largest of its arguments, and `min` the smallest.
higher.lesson.10: A **filter** keeps only the elements for which a predicate is true. Many Scheme systems have a `filter` procedure, but it is not part of R7RS small. You can write your own with recursion. Here it is called `keep`.
higher.lesson.12: A procedure can also return a new procedure. `adder` below returns a `lambda` that remembers the value of `n`.
higher.card.0: Procedures are values: `(define (twice f x) (f (f x)))`
higher.card.1: `(map f '(1 2 3))` gives the list of results
higher.card.2: `(for-each f l)` calls `f` for every element, for actions like printing
higher.card.4: R7RS small has no `filter`: write your own with recursion
higher-1.explain: `map` adds 1 to every element and gives a new list.
higher-3.explain: The `lambda` doubles, and `twice` calls it two times: 5, 10, 20.
higher-4.explain: `(adder 2)` returns a procedure that adds 2, so `(add-two 7)` is 9.
higher-5.explain: `map` multiplies the elements pair by pair: 1 × 4, 2 × 5 and 3 × 6.
higher-6.explain: `keep` keeps the elements for which `odd?` is true: 1, 3 and 5.
higher-7.explain: The last argument of `apply` must be a list. Write `(apply + '(1 2 3))`.
higher-8.explain: `map` gives a new list and does not change `nums`. The code prints `(1 2 3)`.
higher-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `(1 4 9)`.
higher-9.explain: `map` gives a list with the result for every element. `for-each` gives no useful result.
higher-10.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 8.
higher-10.explain: `(apply max '(5 3 8))` is `(max 5 3 8)`, which gives the largest number, 8.
higher-11.prompt: Build an expression that adds up the numbers in the list `prices`.
higher-11.explain: `apply` passes the elements of `prices` to `+` as arguments.
higher-12.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
higher-12.pairs.0: gives a list with the result for every element
higher-12.pairs.1: calls a procedure for every element, for actions
higher-12.pairs.2: calls a procedure with the elements of a list as arguments
higher-12.pairs.3: creates a procedure without a name
data.title: Strings, vectors and association lists
data.summary: Work with string procedures and characters, store values in vectors, and look up values in association lists.
data.lesson.0: Scheme has many procedures for strings. `string-length` counts the characters. `(substring s start end)` gives a part of the string, from position `start` up to, but not including, `end`. Positions start at 0. `string-upcase` gives the string in capital letters, and `string=?` compares two strings.
data.lesson.2: A string is made of **characters**. You write a single character as `#\a`. `string-ref` gives the character at a position. `string->list` turns a string into a list of characters, and `list->string` turns it back. `string->number` turns a string into a number.
data.lesson.5: A **vector** holds values in order, like a list, but you can reach every element directly by its position. `(vector 5 10 15)` creates a vector, and `display` shows it as `#(5 10 15)`. `vector-ref` gets an element, and `vector-length` counts the elements.
data.lesson.7: `(make-vector 3 0)` creates a vector with 3 elements that are all 0. `vector-set!` changes an element. The `!` at the end of a name means that the procedure changes something. `vector->list` turns a vector into a list.
data.lesson.9: Do not change values that you wrote with a quote or as literals, like `'(1 2 3)`, `#(1 2 3)` or `"text"`. When you want to change a vector, create it with `vector` or `make-vector`.
data.lesson.11: An **association list** is a list of pairs: each pair has a key and a value, like `(bo . 7)`. `(assoc key alist)` gives the first pair whose key is `equal?` to `key`, or `#f` if there is none. The `cdr` of the pair is the value. Keys are often symbols, but strings and numbers work too.
data.lesson.13: Because `assoc` gives `#f` for a missing key, check the result before you take its `cdr`: `(let ((p (assoc key ages))) (if p (cdr p) 0))` gives 0 for unknown names.
data-1.explain: Positions 3, 4, 5 and 6 hold `g`, `r`, `a` and `m`. Position 7 is not included.
data-2.explain: The space counts as a character too: 5 + 1 + 5 is 11.
data-3.explain: `vector-set!` replaces the element at position 1, which is the second one.
data-4.explain: `assoc` finds the pair `(green . 2)`, and its `cdr` is 2.
data-5.explain: Position 2 holds the character `t`. `write` shows a character the way you write it in code: `#\t`.
data-6.explain: No pair has the key `z`, so `assoc` gives `#f`.
data-7.explain: Positions start at 0, so position 1 holds 5.
data-8.explain: `string=?` compares exactly, and small and capital letters are different characters.
data-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `HELLO`.
data-9.explain: `string-upcase` gives the string in capital letters.
data-10.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 2.
data-10.explain: `assoc` gives the pair `(pears . 2)`. Its `car` is the key and its `cdr` is the value 2.
data-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `#(5 6 7)`.
data-11.explain: Each element is one more than the element before it, so position 0 must be set first, then 1, then 2.
data-12.prompt: The program should print `10` and `30`. Which line has the bug?
data-12.explain: The vector has 3 elements at the positions 0, 1 and 2. The last one is `(vector-ref v 2)`.
